desc:
You are at the top-left cell (0, 0) of a grid at time 0. Every cell contains a gate: grid[r][c] is the earliest time at which you are allowed to step into that cell (grid[0][0] = 0).

Each second you must move to one of the four side-adjacent cells; you cannot stay in place. A move that starts at second t puts you in the new cell at second t + 1, and it is allowed only if t + 1 ≥ grid[new row][new col]. You may walk back and forth between cells (for example to wait for a gate to open).

Return the earliest second at which you can be in the bottom-right cell, or -1 if it is impossible. If the grid has one cell, the answer is 0.

grid = [[0, 1, 3],
        [3, 2, 2]]
second 1: (0,1)   second 2: (1,1)   second 3: (1,2)  -> 3
grid = [[0, 5],
        [4, 1]]
neither neighbour can be entered at second 1  -> -1
hints: First decide when the answer is impossible. At second 1 you must already be moving. What does that say about the two neighbours of (0, 0)?
If you can make the first move, you can bounce between your current cell and the previous one forever, so waiting is always possible - but only in steps of 2 seconds.

Run Dijkstra on cells with the earliest arrival time. To enter a neighbour with gate g at candidate time t + 1: if g ≤ t + 1 use t + 1; otherwise use g when (g - (t + 1)) is even and g + 1 when it is odd.
editorial: If neither the cell to the right nor the cell below the start can be entered at second 1 (both have gate > 1), you can never leave the start cell, so the answer is -1. Otherwise you can always step to such a neighbour and back, so you can kill time two seconds at a time, and every gate eventually opens for good (gates only open, never close again).

Dijkstra on the cells works with a small twist. Arriving at a cell u at time t, a neighbour v with gate g can be entered at time t + 1 if g ≤ t + 1. Otherwise you have to wait: bouncing changes your arrival time by multiples of 2, so the earliest valid arrival is g when (g - (t + 1)) is even and g + 1 when it is odd. Arriving earlier is never worse because you can always burn extra time later in steps of 2 (but not 1), which the parity rule already accounts for.

Process cells with a min-heap keyed by arrival time; the first time the bottom-right cell is popped, its time is the answer. Each cell is relaxed at most four times, so the time is O(R C log(R C)). With R = C = 60 this is tiny.
